---
title: "Build a local development workflow that stays predictable"
date: 2026-04-11
categories: [development]
tags: [local-development, ddev, task, git-hooks]
summary: "You will set up a local development workflow that gives your project one command surface, repeatable services, and fast verification before commit."
slug: "build-a-local-development-workflow-that-stays-predictable"
draft: true
---

Ahnii!

This post shows you how to build a local development workflow with [DDEV](https://ddev.readthedocs.io/), [Task](https://taskfile.dev/), and [Lefthook](https://lefthook.dev/) so your project starts the same way, runs the same checks, and stays easier to trust.

## Prerequisites

- [Docker](https://www.docker.com/) running on your machine
- [Git](https://git-scm.com/) installed
- A project with an application server, tests, and a formatter or linter
- [Task](https://taskfile.dev/) installed locally
- [DDEV](https://ddev.readthedocs.io/) installed locally
- [Lefthook](https://lefthook.dev/) installed locally

## Give Your Project One Command Surface

If your local workflow depends on memory, it will drift. You need one place where common tasks live, but that only works if every command there is worth keeping.

Create a `Taskfile.yml` at the root of your project:

```yaml
version: '3'

tasks:
  setup:
    desc: Install dependencies and start local services
    cmds:
      - ddev start
      - ddev exec composer install
      - ddev exec npm install

  dev:
    desc: Start the application in local development
    cmds:
      - ddev launch

  test:
    desc: Run the test suite
    cmds:
      - ddev exec php artisan test

  lint:
    desc: Run formatting and static checks
    cmds:
      - ddev exec composer pint --test
      - ddev exec npm run lint

  check:
    desc: Run the full local verification pass
    cmds:
      - task: lint
      - task: test
```

This gives you a small command surface that you can remember: `task setup`, `task dev`, and `task check`. It also keeps your team from inventing five different ways to run the same project.

A command surface alone is not enough, though. If the services behind those commands vary from machine to machine, your workflow still breaks in practice.

## Run Services in a Repeatable Container Setup

A local workflow is easier to keep stable when your app, database, and runtime live behind the same tool. You do not need a complicated setup. You need one that starts cleanly and stays boring.

Start with a minimal DDEV config:

```yaml
name: app

type: php
ndocroot: public
php_version: "8.3"
webserver_type: nginx-fpm
router_http_port: "80"
router_https_port: "443"

aadditional_hostnames: []
aadditional_fqdns: []
database:
  type: mariadb
  version: "10.11"
```

This tells DDEV which stack to boot and which runtime your project expects. Once it is in place, `ddev start` becomes the stable entry point your other commands can depend on.

If your project needs background work, add those commands to DDEV too:

```yaml
web_extra_daemons:
  - name: vite
    command: npm run dev
    directory: /var/www/html
```

This keeps your frontend watcher inside the same local environment instead of leaving it as an extra terminal tab you have to remember. That matters even more once you start adding automated checks.

## Block Bad Commits With Git Hooks

You should not rely on memory right before a commit. Your workflow should stop you before broken code lands, but it should do that fast enough that you keep it enabled.

Create a `lefthook.yml` file:

```yaml
pre-commit:
  parallel: true
  commands:
    php-format:
      run: ddev exec composer pint --test
    js-lint:
      run: ddev exec npm run lint

pre-push:
  commands:
    tests:
      run: task test
```

This runs cheap checks before commit and leaves the slower test suite for push. You get fast feedback locally, and you stop shipping obvious failures upstream.

Install the hooks once:

```bash
lefthook install
```

This writes the Git hook scripts that call your Lefthook configuration. After that, the checks run automatically when you commit or push.

You now have one command surface and one execution environment. The next question is whether the whole thing actually behaves the way you expect.

## Verify the Local Workflow Works

Do one clean pass from setup to verification. If any step feels awkward, fix that now instead of teaching your future self a workaround.

```bash
task setup
task dev
task check
```

`task setup` should start your containers and install dependencies. `task dev` should open or start your app, and `task check` should give you one place to confirm the project is ready for commit.

If you want a quick sanity check before you touch real work, make a throwaway change and let the hooks catch it:

```bash
git checkout -b workflow-smoke-test
echo "// smoke test" >> resources/js/app.js
git add resources/js/app.js
git commit -m "test hooks"
```

This confirms your hooks are active and your local checks actually run at commit time. If the commit passes when it should fail, your workflow still has a gap.

## Keep the Workflow Small as the Project Grows

A local workflow should remove decisions, not create new ones. When you add a command, ask whether it belongs in `Taskfile.yml`, whether it should run inside DDEV, and whether it needs hook enforcement.

That gives you a simple rule set:

- Put repeatable project commands in `Taskfile.yml`
- Run app services and project tooling through DDEV
- Use Lefthook for fast checks that protect commits and pushes
- Keep `task check` as the one command that tells you whether your branch is healthy

If you hold that line, your workflow stays teachable. It also stays easier to debug because every moving part has a clear job.

---
title: "Local-first development starts on your machine"
date: 2026-04-11
categories: [development]
tags: [local-first, workflow, developer-experience]
summary: "Learn what local-first development means, why it keeps your feedback loop short, and who benefits from building this way."
slug: "local-first-development-starts-on-your-machine"
draft: true
---

Ahnii!

[Local-first development](https://www.inkandswitch.com/local-first/) keeps your project usable on your machine first, which matters when you want faster feedback and fewer environment surprises.

You do not need a perfect cloud stack to make progress.

You need a setup that lets you open the app, change the code, refresh, and trust what you see.

That sounds small. It changes everything.

When your database, assets, and dev server all depend on a remote service, your work starts with waiting. You wait for a tunnel. You wait for a container pull. You wait for credentials to stop expiring. By the time the page loads, you have already spent attention on the wrong problem.

Local-first development pulls that loop back onto your machine. Your app runs where you are working. Your data stays close enough to inspect. Your failures show up early, in a place you can actually debug. But speed is only part of the story.

## Why local-first development keeps your feedback loop short

A short feedback loop helps you notice cause and effect.

You change a route. You reload the page. You see the break. Then you fix it before the mistake spreads into three more files and a vague bug report.

That rhythm is hard to keep when every test run depends on a distant system. You can still build that way, but you start treating delay as normal. The next part is where that cost shows up most clearly.

---
title: "Turn a one-off task into a repeatable workflow"
date: 2026-04-11
categories: [workflow, writing]
tags: [workflow, documentation, process]
summary: "Learn how to turn a task you keep repeating into a short workflow you can follow and teach."
slug: "turn-a-one-off-task-into-a-repeatable-workflow"
draft: true
---

Ahnii!

This post shows you how to turn a task you keep repeating into a short workflow you can follow, check, and hand to someone else without rewriting it every time.

## Prerequisites

- A task you have done at least twice
- A place to write the steps down
- Ten quiet minutes to remove the guesswork

## Turn One Task Into Four Stable Steps

A repeatable workflow starts small.

You do not need a full system first. You need the version you can trust on a busy day.

Start by writing the task as four steps: prepare, do the work, verify the result, record what changed. That shape is easy to remember, but it is also strict enough to catch the parts you usually skip.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Prepare] --> B[Do the work]
    B --> C[Verify the result]
    C --> D[Record what changed]
```

This flow gives the work a fixed order. It also gives you a clear place to stop when something fails.

{{< steps >}}
{{< step "Prepare the starting point" >}}
Write down what must already be true before you begin. Name the files, commands, inputs, or approvals you need.
{{< /step >}}
{{< step "Do one bounded action" >}}
Keep the core action narrow. If the step contains three different jobs, split it now instead of hiding the complexity.
{{< /step >}}
{{< step "Verify the result" >}}
Check the output right away. Do not trust memory, and do not leave verification for the end.
{{< /step >}}
{{< step "Record the outcome" >}}
Leave a short note about what changed, what failed, or what needs follow-up. The next run gets easier because this run left a trail.
{{< /step >}}
{{< /steps >}}

That structure keeps your workflow readable, but plain structure is not enough. The language has to stay sharp too.

If you want the steps to be usable, write them like this:

```text
1. Open the file you need to change.
2. Update the value.
3. Run the check.
4. Save the result in your notes.
```

Each line carries one action. The sequence is obvious, so the reader does not have to decode it.

Now compare that with a version that sounds busy but says less:

```text
Open the relevant file and make the necessary updates based on your current task,
then perform whatever validation makes sense so you can ensure everything looks
correct before documenting anything important for later.
```

The second version drifts. It hides the action, stretches the sentence, and leaves too much for the reader to interpret.

Short sentences help, but you still need rhythm.

If every line is the same length, the section turns flat. If every paragraph lands the same way, the reader starts skimming. Change the pace on purpose. Use one short sentence when you need emphasis. Follow it with a longer one when you need to explain the tradeoff.

That is the whole move.

You are not trying to sound clever. You are trying to make the next pass faster, cleaner, and harder to misunderstand. Once you can do that in one section, you can carry the same pattern into a full guide.

## Verify Your Workflow Before You Reuse It

Run the workflow exactly as written.

Do not fill gaps from memory. If a step only works because you already know what it meant, the workflow is incomplete.

A good check is simple: hand the draft to your future self. If you can follow it a week later without guessing, keep it. If not, tighten the verbs, split the crowded steps, and remove any sentence that sounds helpful but does not change what the reader does next.

---
title: "Rewrite vague development notes into concrete process steps"
date: 2026-04-11
categories: [writing, development-process]
tags: [writing, docs, process, editing]
summary: "You will turn vague development notes into clear process language your team can act on."
slug: "rewrite-vague-development-notes"
draft: true
---

Ahnii!

This post shows you how to turn vague development notes into clear process steps so your team can act on them without guessing.

## Prerequisites

- A draft set of development notes, handoff notes, or retro notes
- Enough context to name the actual step, owner, or outcome

## Replace vague process language with concrete actions

If your notes say a process created "momentum" or made work "seamless," stop and ask one question: what changed in the work itself?

That question gives you the next draft. You are not polishing tone yet. You are naming behavior.

```markdown
The new workflow created momentum across the team.
Handoffs are now seamless.
The release checklist is robust.
This update was transformative for delivery.
```

These lines sound positive, but they do not tell your reader what happened. A teammate cannot repeat the process from this version.

```markdown
The team moved deployment steps into one checklist in the repo.
Developers now open the same release document before tagging a version.
QA signs off in the pull request instead of a separate chat thread.
That cut missed release steps because everyone works from the same list.
```

This version gives you actions, location, and outcome. Your reader can see what changed, and the next question becomes more useful: what still breaks?

## Use a simple rewrite pattern for each fuzzy sentence

When you find vague words in your notes, rewrite each sentence with four parts: who did the work, what changed, where it happens, and what result followed.

{{< compare >}}
{{< before >}}
The process is now seamless and robust.
{{< /before >}}
{{< after >}}
Developers add migration notes to the pull request template, and reviewers check them before merge. That catches missing rollback steps earlier.
{{< /after >}}
{{< /compare >}}

The "after" version works because it names the step and the effect. Once you can do that for one sentence, you can clean the rest of the section the same way.

## Verify your process notes before you publish them

Read each sentence and check whether a new teammate could follow it without asking you what you meant. If the answer is no, the sentence still needs one more pass.

You do not need bigger words. You need clearer ones.

# The Bridge on the River Kwai (1957) — ★★★★

*Directed by David Lean. Starring Alec Guinness, William Holden, Jack Hawkins, Sessue Hayakawa. 161 min.*

---

The genius of *The Bridge on the River Kwai* is that it understands war can destroy men just as thoroughly through pride as through bullets. David Lean sets up what looks like a prison-camp survival story, then turns it into something stranger and better: a film about officers so committed to duty, prestige, and procedure that they lose sight of what side they are even serving. It is a big, handsome war movie, but its real battlefield is the mind.

The central performance is Alec Guinness as Colonel Nicholson, and the movie works because Guinness never plays him as a simple fool. In the early camp scenes, when Nicholson refuses to let his officers perform manual labor and endures punishment rather than bend to Saito, the film has the hard edge of a clash between military codes. Those scenes are excellent because both men believe they are defending civilization. Sessue Hayakawa gives Saito real exhaustion and humiliation, not cartoon cruelty, and the result is a power struggle that feels more dangerous than a firefight.

What makes the picture memorable is the slow, unsettling shift once Nicholson begins overseeing construction of the bridge. Lean stages these sequences with almost procedural fascination. You watch lines get surveyed, timbers raised, and discipline restored, and for a while it feels perversely triumphant. That is exactly the point. The bridge becomes a symbol of professional pride detached from moral sense. By the time Nicholson is admiring the finished structure, the film has quietly turned into a critique of the officer class and the habits of empire.

For a war film, the combat is limited, but the tension is superbly handled. The final sabotage sequence works because you understand the terrain, the stakes, and the tactical problem at every step. When Shears, Warden, and the commandos move into position, Lean keeps the geography clear in a way many larger battle films still fail to do. The suspense comes from timing, visibility, and Nicholson's dawning realization, not from noise. That clarity gives the climax its force.

Historically, the film takes liberties, especially in its portrayal of Japanese command and in the psychology of the British prisoners, and it is better treated as a moral drama than a faithful reconstruction of the Burma railway. Still, it respects the larger reality that war production, hierarchy, and ego can become their own kind of madness. The period detail, jungle photography, and physical scale of the production still hold up. Nothing feels synthetic. You believe in the heat, the mud, and the sheer labor of the place.

What lingers is the film's perspective on war itself. This is not a movie about glory. It is about intelligent, disciplined men walking themselves into absurdity because they cannot imagine stepping outside the systems that formed them. That makes it worth revisiting, and it also sends you back to the history, which is always a good sign. If you like war films that care as much about command psychology as explosions, this is essential viewing.

★★★★

---
title: "Turning a Coding Session Into a Blog Draft That People Will Actually Read"
date: 2026-04-11
categories: [cursor]
tags: [claude-code, blogging, workflow]
summary: "A simple way to turn a messy coding session into a clear blog draft with a problem, approach, solution, and takeaway."
slug: "turning-a-coding-session-into-a-blog-draft"
draft: true
---

## The Problem / Context

A good coding session usually does not look good on paper.

It is messy. You try one thing, hit an edge case, inspect a few files, realize your first assumption was wrong, and only then find the version of the solution worth keeping. That is exactly what makes the session useful, but it is also why so many potentially good technical posts never get written. The raw material exists, but it is trapped in terminal output, half-finished thoughts, and a pile of edits that only made sense while I was in the middle of them.

What I wanted was a reliable way to take that session and turn it into something blog-shaped without pretending the work was cleaner than it really was. Not a polished marketing recap. A technical draft with enough structure that someone else could follow the arc from problem to outcome and actually learn something from it.

## What I Tried / The Approach

The first mistake is trying to write chronologically from the full session log.

That sounds reasonable, but it usually produces a bad post. Terminal sessions are full of low-signal steps: repeated searches, dead ends that are not interesting, and implementation details that mattered in the moment but do not matter to a reader. If I start with the raw transcript and try to preserve everything, I end up writing a diary instead of a post.

What worked better was extracting the session into four questions:

1. What was the actual problem?
2. What did I try before the final fix?
3. What changed that made it work?
4. What would I tell someone doing this again?

That sounds obvious, but it forces the right kind of compression. A blog post is not a session replay. It is a useful retelling.

I also found that the most valuable material often sits in the wrong turns. If I changed direction because a test failed, because a framework assumption was wrong, or because a seemingly clean abstraction turned out to be too clever, that belongs in the draft. Readers do not just need the final code. They need the decision points.

The practical workflow I settled into looks like this:

```text
- identify the strongest problem -> solution arc
- discard low-signal steps
- keep one or two failed attempts if they taught something
- pull in small code snippets that show the real change
- end with the rule or pattern I would reuse next time
```

That last point matters. If the session does not produce a reusable lesson, it usually does not deserve a full post.

## The Solution

The simplest useful output was a draft template that forces the session into a clear narrative shape.

I start with front matter so the post is immediately publishable later, even if it stays a draft for a while:

```yaml
---
title: "Turning a Coding Session Into a Blog Draft That People Will Actually Read"
date: 2026-04-11
categories: [cursor]
tags: [claude-code, blogging, workflow]
summary: "A simple way to turn a messy coding session into a clear blog draft with a problem, approach, solution, and takeaway."
slug: "turning-a-coding-session-into-a-blog-draft"
draft: true
---
```

Then I write the body in four sections.

The first section is not "what I built." It is the friction. What was failing? What was unclear? What was costing time? If that part is weak, the rest of the post usually feels weightless.

The second section captures the investigation. This is where I include the first assumption, the check that disproved it, and the trade-off that shaped the next move. I do not need every command. I need the commands or observations that changed my understanding.

A small snippet like this is usually enough to make the session feel concrete:

```bash
rg "session-to-blog" /home/jones/dev/skills
ls /home/fsd42/dev/blog/content/posts/*/
grep -rl "workflow" /home/fsd42/dev/blog/content/posts/
```

Those commands are not interesting by themselves. What matters is why they were run: to find the skill, understand its constraints, and avoid writing something that duplicates an existing post.

The third section is the working shape of the solution. That can be code, a content structure, a shell workflow, or a pattern. In this case, the solution was a repeatable content transformation:

```markdown
## The Problem / Context
(What happened and why it mattered)

## What I Tried / The Approach
(Investigation, false starts, trade-offs)

## The Solution
(What changed and why it worked)

## What I Learned
(Reusable takeaway)
```

That structure is plain on purpose. It keeps me from drifting into filler, and it keeps the reader oriented. They can skim it in seconds and still understand the arc.

The other thing I changed was how I handled tone. If I write like I am documenting for myself, the draft becomes stiff. If I write like I am explaining the problem to another engineer right after solving it, the draft gets better fast. That usually means first person, shorter transitions, and a willingness to say, "I tried the obvious version first, and it was wrong."

That kind of sentence does more work than a polished paragraph pretending the right answer was obvious from the start.

## What I Learned

A useful technical post is not the same thing as a complete record.

The session can stay messy. The draft should not. What matters is preserving the logic of the work: the original problem, the key checks, the turning point, and the final rule I would reuse next time.

The biggest change for me was treating the failed attempt as part of the value, not as something to hide. In a real coding session, the first idea is often incomplete. That is normal. If the correction taught me something, it belongs in the post.

I would also keep the scope narrower than feels natural. One focused post about a specific debugging path, migration decision, or workflow pattern is almost always better than a giant recap of everything that happened in a long session. A reader can apply one sharp lesson. They usually will not retain ten loose ones.

If I were doing this again, I would capture the candidate blog angle before the session ends, while the problem still feels vivid. Even one line is enough: "This got interesting when the first assumption failed and the fix came from changing the structure, not the syntax." That note makes the draft much easier to write later.

The takeaway is simple: do not try to publish the transcript. Find the arc. Keep the real decision points. Show the working change. End with the lesson. That is usually enough to turn a good coding session into a post worth reading.

Ahnii!

I spent a recent build session tightening the shape of my work instead of adding another shiny feature. I needed a clearer line between what I am building, why I am building it, and how the pieces actually fit together when the day gets messy. That session pulled me back to the center of it. I am not trying to make a pile of disconnected tools. I am building a system I can live inside.

## The Problem / The Why

A lot of my recent work has been moving between [Waaseyaa](https://waaseyaa.org), [Minoo](https://minoo.live), and [OIATC](https://oiatc.waaseyaa.org). On a good day, that feels connected. On a bad day, it can feel like context switching disguised as progress. I can tell when that starts happening because I spend more time naming things, reorganizing things, and thinking about future architecture than I spend finishing what is in front of me.

This build session was about cutting through that.

I needed to see the work as it really is. Waaseyaa is the foundation. It is the framework work, the infrastructure thinking, the system underneath. Minoo is closer to people. It is where community, communication, and daily use start to show up. OIATC carries a different weight for me because it sits closer to governance, knowledge, and Indigenous institutional capacity. Those are different surfaces, but they are part of one direction.

What I was trying to solve was not only technical. It was conceptual. If I cannot describe the relationship between these projects in plain language, then I am probably carrying too much abstraction in my head. That makes the work harder than it needs to be.

## What I Built / What I Found

The session turned into a kind of cleanup and re-alignment. I worked through the structure of the projects, the naming, and the places where I had allowed ambiguity to pile up. Some of that was code. Some of it was documentation. Some of it was me staring at a decision long enough to admit that I had been avoiding the simpler answer.

What I found is that my best sessions happen when I stop pretending every part of the system needs equal attention. It does not. Some parts need to be stable. Some parts need to be tested by real use. Some parts need to wait.

That matters because I have a habit that I think a lot of builders have. I can keep extending the frame forever. Another layer. Another refactor. Another round of planning that feels responsible but delays contact with reality. This time I pushed in the other direction. I looked for the next piece that would make the system more usable, more legible, or more true to its purpose.

I also found myself thinking again about Indigenous digital sovereignty, not as a slogan but as a practical demand. If I am serious about that, then the work cannot just be expressive. It has to be durable. It has to be maintainable. It has to make sense to the people who will inherit it, use it, or build with it after me. That changes how I judge a good session. A good session is not one where I produce the most code. It is one where the path gets clearer.

By the end of the day, I felt that clarity returning. The projects looked less like separate tabs in my brain and more like parts of a shared effort. That is a small result on paper, maybe. In practice, it is the difference between wandering and building.

## Where It's Going

The next step is not to explode the scope again. The next step is to keep moving in smaller, sharper increments. I want Waaseyaa to keep getting stronger at the foundation level. I want Minoo to keep getting closer to real community use. I want OIATC to keep becoming something that can hold serious work without losing the values underneath it.

I am trying to stay honest about pace. Some pieces are ready to move. Some are still forming. I would rather say that plainly than talk like every week is a breakthrough.

If you want to follow the build, stay with me here. Subscribe if you want to see where this work is going, or reply if something in this direction resonates with you.

# Typed Fields

Typed fields are how you attach structured data to your entities in [Waaseyaa](https://github.com/waaseyaa/framework).

## Install the Field Package

```bash
composer require waaseyaa/fields
```

This installs the field package in your project with [Composer](https://getcomposer.org/). You can then register field definitions on any entity type.

## Define Your Entity Type

```php
<?php

use Waaseyaa\Entities\EntityType;
use Waaseyaa\Fields\Field;

return EntityType::make('article')
    ->label('Article')
    ->fields([
        Field::text('title')->required(),
        Field::slug('slug')->unique(),
        Field::longText('body'),
        Field::boolean('published')->default(false),
    ]);
```

This defines an `article` entity with four typed fields. Each field carries its own validation and storage rules.

## Save Data Through the Entity API

```php
<?php

$article = entity('article')->create([
    'title' => 'Spring Gathering Notes',
    'slug' => 'spring-gathering-notes',
    'body' => 'Council updates and community planning notes.',
    'published' => true,
]);

$article->save();
```

This creates a new entity and writes it through the same API you use everywhere else. The framework validates the field values before storage.

## Read Typed Values Back

```php
<?php

$article = entity('article')->findBy('slug', 'spring-gathering-notes');

echo $article->title;
echo $article->published ? 'yes' : 'no';
```

This loads the entity and returns values in the shape your field definitions describe. You do not need a separate mapping layer for common reads.

## Add Field Rules Where They Matter

```php
<?php

Field::text('title')
    ->required()
    ->minLength(10)
    ->maxLength(120);
```

This keeps the rule next to the field it governs. When you change the field definition, you change validation in the same place.

## Use Typed Fields When Your Data Has Structure

Use typed fields when your content needs validation, consistent storage, and predictable reads. Blog posts, directory listings, case records, and internal tools all benefit from the same pattern.

# Configure Your Workflow

This section shows you how to define a workflow, load it into your app, and override values per environment.

## Define Your Base Configuration

Start with one file that describes the workflow you want to run. Keep the default path simple. Put the values you expect to share across local, staging, and production in one place.

```yaml
workflow:
  name: content-sync
  schedule: "0 */6 * * *"
  source: s3
  retries: 3
  notifications:
    email: ops@example.com
    slack: false
```

This file gives your workflow a name, a schedule, and a small set of runtime options. You use it as the base layer, then override only the values that need to change per environment.

## Load Configuration at Startup

Read the base file when your app boots. Fail early if the file is missing or malformed.

```php
<?php

$config = yaml_parse_file(__DIR__ . '/config/workflow.yaml');

if ($config === false) {
    throw new RuntimeException('Unable to load workflow configuration.');
}

$workflow = $config['workflow'];
```

This loads the YAML file into memory and pulls out the `workflow` section. The runtime exception stops startup before you run a job with incomplete settings.

## Override Values Per Environment

You usually need a different schedule, destination, or notification target outside local development. Use environment variables for that layer. They are easy to change and easy to inspect.

```php
<?php

$workflow['schedule'] = getenv('WORKFLOW_SCHEDULE') ?: $workflow['schedule'];
$workflow['source'] = getenv('WORKFLOW_SOURCE') ?: $workflow['source'];
$workflow['notifications']['email'] = getenv('WORKFLOW_EMAIL') ?: $workflow['notifications']['email'];
```

This keeps your committed config stable while letting each environment supply its own values. If an override is not present, the base config stays in place.

## Validate Required Settings

Do not trust input just because it came from config. Check the values before you start the workflow.

```php
<?php

if (empty($workflow['name'])) {
    throw new InvalidArgumentException('Workflow name is required.');
}

if (!is_numeric($workflow['retries']) || $workflow['retries'] < 0) {
    throw new InvalidArgumentException('Retries must be zero or greater.');
}
```

These checks catch bad data close to the source. You avoid vague runtime failures later when the worker tries to execute.

## Inspect the Final Runtime Configuration

Print the merged result once during development. That gives you a quick way to confirm which values actually made it through.

```bash
php bin/show-workflow-config
```

Run this command after you change either the YAML file or your environment variables. You should see the final values the app will use, not just the defaults you started with.

## Keep Secrets Out of the Base File

Do not store tokens, passwords, or private keys in the shared config file. Put secrets in your environment or secret manager, then inject them when the app starts.

```php
<?php

$workflow['credentials'] = [
    'key' => getenv('WORKFLOW_API_KEY'),
    'secret' => getenv('WORKFLOW_API_SECRET'),
];
```

This keeps sensitive values out of version control. It also lets you rotate credentials without changing the base workflow definition.

# Package Overview

[This package](#package-overview) gives you one place to handle a specific job in your application. You install it, configure it, and call it from your code without building the same plumbing again.

## Use This Package

You use this package when you want a clear API for a repeated task. It handles the common workflow, keeps the moving parts in one place, and lets you focus on your application code.

## Understand What It Does

You get a small set of focused features. The package accepts input, applies its rules, and returns a predictable result. You do not need extra setup beyond the required configuration.

## Fit It Into Your Project

You can add the package to an existing codebase without changing how the rest of your application works. It is meant to sit at one boundary, do its job, and stay out of the way.

## Configure Only What You Need

You start with the default behavior, then override the parts that matter for your project. If your use case is simple, you can keep the configuration small. If your use case is more specific, you can adjust the available options directly.

## Read the API Quickly

The public surface stays narrow. You should be able to scan the main entry points, understand what each one accepts, and know what comes back.

## Expect Predictable Behavior

The package favors explicit inputs and explicit outputs. If something fails, you should see where it failed and what to change. That makes it easier to test, debug, and maintain.

## Start With the Core Workflow

Install the package. Add your configuration. Call the main API from the part of your app that needs it. If you need deeper integration, expand from that baseline instead of wiring everything at once.
